title: Per-stats oldest_ts_ms / row_count are O(symbols x bars) under the store lock, called on every stats() poll
evidence: oldest_ts_ms (534-543) scans every symbol's bar dict computing min(); stats() (545-568) additionally does row_count = sum(len(...)) over all symbols and calls oldest_ts_ms — all under self._lock. newest_ts_ms is O(1) (cached _global_max_ts_ms) but oldest is not cached. At ~673 symbols x ~1000+ bars this is a multi-hundred-thousand-element scan holding the store lock; manager.stats() (kline_stream_manager.py:300-301) calls store.stats() and is exposed via the daemon's stats endpoint, so an operator/telemetry poll stalls every WS bar insert for the duration of the scan.
impact: latency: lock-held O(N) scan on a telemetry path can stall WS inserts during the hourly ~566-symbol burst; no correctness impact.
proposed_fix: Maintain an incremental _global_min_ts_ms (or recompute lazily off eviction) the same way _global_max_ts_ms is cached, and compute row_count incrementally, so stats() is O(symbols) at most and ideally O(1).

verdict.reasoning: Code matches the finding. oldest_ts_ms (kline_store.py:534-543) scans every symbol computing min(symbol_bars) per symbol — O(total bars) — while holding self._lock (an RLock). stats() (545-568) calls oldest_ts_ms() under the same lock. newest_ts_ms() is O(1) via the cached _global_max_ts_ms, so the asymmetry the finding describes is real. At the live default retain_days=90 (kline_stream_manager.py:90) a symbol holds ~2160 1h bars; at ~673 symbols the min-scan touches ~1.45M dict keys, plausibly tens of ms while the store lock blocks WS add_bar. manager.stats() -> store.stats() is reachable (kline_stream_manager.py:301) and called from event_demo_daemon.py:598 and long_native daemon:446.\n\nTwo caveats that cap the severity at low/minor and partially refute the impact framing: (1) the row_count = sum(len(...)) term the finding lists as an additional cost is actually cheap — len() on a dict is O(1), so row_count is O(symbols) (~673 trivial calls), not a real cost driver; the only genuine O(N) cost is the oldest_ts_ms min-scan. (2) store.stats() is NOT a hammered telemetry endpoint — it is polled once per ~60s cycle plus once at startup, not per-second. The hourly insert burst (~566 symbols) and a 60s-cadence poll rarely coincide, and a collision merely queues inserts behind a sub-second scan with no dropped bars and zero correctness impact (pybit buffers; inserts just wait on the RLock). So this is a real but minor latency papercut, consistent with the consistency-gap pattern the codebase already optimizes elsewhere (_global_max_ts_ms cache, amortized eviction, window cache).
verdict.fix_notes: The fix DIRECTION is sound but the literal proposal ("maintain an incremental _global_min_ts_ms the same way _global_max_ts_ms is cached") is an oversimplification that would introduce a correctness bug if applied naively. The max cache is trivially incremental because inserts only RAISE the max and eviction NEVER removes the newest bar. The minimum is the opposite case: _evict_old_locked (365-377) exists precisely to delete the oldest bars, so any cached min is invalidated on every eviction. A naive 'mirror the max' implementation that only updates min on insert (min(new, current)) would return a stale, too-old oldest_ts after eviction — a wrong stat. The correct approach is the alternative the finding itself names: recompute the global min lazily inside _evict_old_locked, which already iterates every symbol, so the min recompute is folded into the existing pass at near-zero extra cost; on the insert path only lower the cached min if the new bar is older. The row_count half (an incremental counter bumped on insert/evict) is safe and simple. Any implementation must preserve the exact stats() schema keys 'oldest_ts_ms' and 'rows' and the None-when-empty semantics, which are asserted in tests/test_liquidity_migration_kline_store.py (lines 97-99, 434). Recommend implementing the eviction-coupled recompute, not the literal 'same as max' mirror, and gating with the existing store tests. Low priority given the minor, poll-frequency-bounded impact.

title: BybitPublicTickerStream has no staleness watchdog or self-reconnect; relies solely on pybit internal reconnect
evidence: BybitPublicTickerStream (bybit.py:758-787) only opens a pybit WebSocket and fires ticker_stream subscribes; it has no last_message tracking, no watchdog thread, and no reconnect-on-stale path — in stark contrast to BybitKlineStreamPool which tracks last_message_monotonic per connection and runs check_stale_connections/_watchdog_loop (bybit.py:1660-1684) to tear down and rebuild idle connections. The daemon's _check_ws_health (event_demo_daemon.py:876-918) only LOGS ticker silence; it never closes/reopens the ticker stream. So a silently-wedged pybit ticker socket (failed internal reconnect) leaves the ticker WS dead until a process restart, with only the 60s REST reconcile carrying prices — and per finding 1, the global staleness gate hides which symbols went stale.
impact: latency/data-integrity: a dead ticker WS degrades silently to REST-only price freshness (~60s) with no automatic recovery, amplifying findings 1 and 2.
proposed_fix: Add a last_message timestamp + watchdog to BybitPublicTickerStream (mirror the kline pool), and have _check_ws_health actively close_ticker_stream()+_open_ticker_stream() when the WS-only clock exceeds a reconnect threshold rather than only warning.

verdict.reasoning:
All factual claims trace to real code. BybitPublicTickerStream (bybit.py:758-787) genuinely has no last_message tracking, no watchdog thread, and no reconnect-on-stale path — verified by reading the full class. This contrasts with BybitKlineStreamPool, which has the full watchdog stack: per-connection last_message_monotonic (bybit.py:1610), check_stale_connections / _watchdog_loop (bybit.py:1660-1715) that tear down and rebuild idle connections. The daemon's _check_ws_health (event_demo_daemon.py:876-918) only LOGS ticker silence (lines 905-918); it never closes/reopens the ticker stream. The reconcile loop's recovery (line 867) re-opens only when _ticker_stream is None, NOT for a wedged-but-non-None pybit socket. So a silently-wedged ticker WS persists until process restart with no auto-recovery. That part of the finding is correct.

However, the claimed impact ("data-integrity", "amplifying findings 1 and 2") overstates the severity. I traced the actual price consumption path: the cycle reads tickers via _bulk_tickers_from_cache_or_rest (event_demo.py:2182-2201), which falls through to live REST public.get_tickers() whenever the cache is_stale past state_cache_stale_seconds (default 120s). Separately, the 60s REST reconcile (_invoke_state_cache_seeder -> _default_short_state_cache_seeder -> ticker_cache.replace_with_rest_snapshot, event_demo_daemon.py:1237-1238) re-seeds the cache and bumps last_event_monotonic (ws_state_cache.py:485-490, 548-549). Net effect with a dead WS: prices delivered to trading decisions are always either <=60s-fresh (REST-reconciled cache) or live (per-cycle REST fallback). There is NO path where stale prices drive trades, and no correctness/data-integrity failure — only a freshness/latency degradation (sub-second WS pushes downgrade to ~60s reconcile cadence). The system stays functionally correct and self-heals its data freshness via the existing REST reconcile already running on a timer. That makes this an operational/observability gap (no auto-reconnect of a dead ticker socket, only a logged warning), worth low rather than medium — the WS is a latency optimization over a REST path that remains fully live.
verdict.fix_notes: The fix direction is sound and the building blocks exist (_close_ticker_stream + _open_ticker_stream at event_demo_daemon.py:801-833 are already exception-guarded), but it is NOT a side-effect-free drop-in. (1) Having _check_ws_health call _close_ticker_stream()+_open_ticker_stream() on stale would run on the reconcile thread and must replicate the shutdown-race guards the existing seed path already wraps around _open_ticker_stream (lines 788-799): re-check self._shutdown.is_set() before opening and close the just-opened stream if shutdown raced, or it can leak a WS connection past daemon shutdown. (2) Reopen relies on the ticker cache being seeded (_open_ticker_stream early-returns when symbol_count()==0, line 802), so the watchdog reconnect must order itself after the reconcile re-seed (the reconcile already calls the seeder before _check_ws_health at lines 857/874, so this ordering holds — but the dependency is implicit and easy to break). (3) Adding a real last_message watchdog inside BybitPublicTickerStream (mirroring the kline pool) is the more robust half and is low-risk in isolation, but it needs the same per-connection backoff gate the kline pool uses (reconnect_backoff_seconds, bybit.py:1692-1696) to avoid a tight reconnect storm against the venue when pybit is genuinely down. (4) Should gate on seconds_since_last_ws_event() (the WS-only clock, ws_state_cache.py:539-546) NOT seconds_since_last_event(), since the latter is bumped by the REST reconcile and would never fire. Recommend implementing with a dedicated regression test asserting close+reopen fires on WS-only silence and does not leak on shutdown; given low severity (REST fallback already keeps prices <=60s fresh), this is a hardening improvement, not an urgent fix.

title: Continuous daemon stops its fast protective-exit thread AFTER base teardown closes WS/kline/trade resources
evidence: ContinuousDemoDaemon.run() starts the Tier-1 fast protective-exit thread (_start_protective_exit_monitor), then calls super().run(). The base LongNativeDemoDaemon.run() teardown happens inside ITS OWN finally block (long_native_event_demo_daemon.py:374-378: _stop_reconcile_thread / _close_ticker_stream / _stop_kline_stream_manager / _close_ws) which runs and RETURNS before the continuous run()'s own finally (_stop_protective_exit_monitor) executes. So during the entire base teardown window the fast loop is still alive: _run_protective_exit_check() (continuous_demo_daemon.py:293-308) reads self._kline_stream_manager.store(), self._ticker_cache, self._private_state_cache and may call _ensure_trade_router()+submit a reduce-only exit via run_continuous_protective_exit_cycle while the base is concurrently stopping the kline manager and closing the WS/trade streams. The loop only exits on its NEXT iteration check of `while not self._shutdown.is_set()`; a check already in flight when teardown begins touches half-closed resources.
impact: ledger/execution: a protective exit can be submitted (or attempted) against a closing trade router / torn-down kline store during shutdown, risking a submitted-but-unrecorded reduce-only order or a spurious exception burst at SIGTERM. Demo-only and exception-guarded so not catastrophic, but it is a real shutdown-ordering inversion.
proposed_fix: Stop the fast protective-exit thread BEFORE the base teardown. Override the teardown ordering: in ContinuousDemoDaemon.run(), set _shutdown and call _stop_protective_exit_monitor() at the START of the base finally (e.g. override a _pre_teardown hook the base finally invokes first), or restructure so the fast monitor is joined before super().run()'s finally closes WS/kline/trade. At minimum, have _run_protective_exit_check() early-return when self._shutdown.is_set().

verdict.reasoning:
The shutdown-ordering inversion is FACTUALLY REAL. ContinuousDemoDaemon.run() (continuous_demo_daemon.py:215-220) starts the fast protective-exit thread, calls super().run(), and only stops the thread in its OWN finally — which runs AFTER the base LongNativeDemoDaemon.run() finally (long_native_event_demo_daemon.py:374-378: _stop_reconcile_thread / _close_ticker_stream / _stop_kline_stream_manager / _close_ws) has already executed and returned. The fast loop (continuous_demo_daemon.py:259-280) only checks `_shutdown` at the iteration top and right after the heartbeat wait, NOT inside _run_protective_exit_check (282-308), so a check already in flight when SIGTERM lands runs to completion concurrently with base teardown. That part of the finding is correct.

However, the finding's IMPACT is materially overstated, and the concrete harm it asserts does not trace to a real path:
1. "submitted against a closing trade router" is FALSE. The base teardown never closes self._trade_router — it closes self._ws_stream (the private execution stream), the ticker stream, the kline manager, and the reconcile thread. The trade router has its own independent REST client + separate WS-trade client (factory at long_native_event_demo_daemon.py:873-924) and is never torn down in run()'s finally. A submit during the window still hits a live, intact router.
2. kline store: the store reference is fetched at lines 293-295 with a None-guard, and run_continuous_protective_exit_cycle wraps kline_store.get_klines in try/except → empty DataFrame (continuous_demo.py:1231-1234). Concurrent manager.stop() is harmless.
3. execution_event_router.clear_all() (called by _close_ws at line 250) only clears _rows under a lock and does not notify _cond, so an in-flight _wait_for_execution_summary simply falls back to REST/timeout (execution_router.py:104-124). Benign.
4. "submitted-but-unrecorded reduce-only order": the continuous run() finally calls _stop_protective_exit_monitor() which thread.join(timeout=5.0) (continuous_demo_daemon.py:246-252), so the in-flight check is given up to 5s to finish its durable preflight→order-row→trade-row writes (continuous_demo.py:1261/1268-1270) before the process exits. The daemon-thread-killed-mid-write path requires a >5s stall, not the normal case.

Net: a real shutdown-ordering inversion whose only realistic effect is one extra, exception-guarded, normally-recorded protective-exit submit during the SIGTERM drain — demo-only and benign. That is a low-severity cleanliness/correctness defect, not the medium ledger/execution risk claimed.
verdict.fix_notes: The minimal proposed fix — early-return in _run_protective_exit_check() when self._shutdown.is_set() (placed before/at the top of the method, e.g. right after the submit/dry-run guard at line 284 or immediately on entry) — is correct and side-effect-free. _shutdown is only ever set by request_shutdown() on SIGTERM/SIGINT, so the guard changes nothing in normal operation; it only suppresses the protective check during the teardown window, which is exactly the goal. Putting it before the _cycle_mutex.acquire and before the _protective_exit_checks++ keeps telemetry clean. The fuller proposed variant (joining the fast monitor before the base teardown via a _pre_teardown hook) is also viable but requires touching the base run() to invoke a hook inside its finally — more surface area; prefer the early-return. Note: even with the early-return there remains a sub-millisecond TOCTOU between the _shutdown check and the submit, but that residual is far smaller than the current full-teardown window and is acceptable given the router is never torn down. Recommend adding a unit test asserting _run_protective_exit_check is a no-op once _shutdown is set (mirrors the existing test_protective_exit_check_defers_to_running_main_cycle pattern at tests/test_liquidity_migration_continuous_demo.py:711).

title: Fast protective-exit thread joined with only 5s timeout; can be killed mid-order-submit on shutdown
evidence: _stop_protective_exit_monitor() does thread.join(timeout=5.0). The thread runs _run_continuous_protective_exit_cycle which acquires the file lock and SUBMITS exit orders (continuous_demo.py:1186-1265, submit_orders path). If a protective exit submission is in flight at SIGTERM and exceeds the 5s join, join() returns while the thread is still running; the thread is daemon=True (line 236) so it is hard-killed when the process exits. A reduce-only exit order can reach Bybit but its ledger/preflight record write may be interrupted, producing paper/demo-vs-ledger drift that ws_risk must later reconcile.
impact: ledger: order submitted to venue but not durably recorded -> reconcile drift on next start. Bounded by reduce-only semantics and ws_risk reconcile authority, hence medium not high.
proposed_fix: Set _shutdown + _tick_event first (already done in request_shutdown), then join with a timeout >= the order-submit/file-lock budget (mirror the short daemon's _stop_kline_warmer which joins with budget+5s), and/or make the protective check check _shutdown immediately before the submit step so it skips submission once shutdown is requested.

verdict.reasoning:
Traced the concrete path and confirmed the mechanism is real, but the impact is overstated; I land at low, not medium.

CONFIRMED FACTS:
- continuous_demo_daemon.py:235-237 — the protective-exit thread is daemon=True, so it is hard-killed at interpreter exit.
- continuous_demo_daemon.py:246-252 — _stop_protective_exit_monitor() does thread.join(timeout=5.0). It runs in run()'s finally (lines 215-220), i.e. AFTER super().run() returns, so the main loop and its shutdown steps are already done; only this thread may still be live.
- continuous_demo.py:1263-1265 -> _execute_continuous_exits (717-797): per held symbol it calls place_order (BybitTradeRouter, WS-preferred w/ REST fallback retries=2 x 0.5s backoff) then _wait_for_execution_summary up to order_fill_confirm_seconds=2.0s, and loops symbols SEQUENTIALLY. A multi-symbol exit batch (or one symbol under a degraded/retrying network) can exceed 5s, so join() can return while the thread is still mid-loop -> hard-kill on exit. The timing window is real.
- continuous_demo_daemon.py:282-314 (_run_protective_exit_check) has NO _shutdown check immediately before entering the submit cycle, so a check that started just before SIGTERM commits to the full batch.
- Precedent the finding cites is accurate: event_demo_daemon.py:957-965 _stop_kline_warmer joins with _kline_warm_budget_seconds + 5.0 with an explicit "can't block shutdown forever, but give it the budget" comment — and that thread does NOT even submit orders, yet gets a budget-aware join, while the order-submitting protective thread gets a flat 5.0.

WHY LOW, NOT MEDIUM — the durability ordering largely defangs the drift claim:
- The finding asserts "order submitted but ledger/preflight record write may be interrupted." But continuous_demo.py:1260-1261 writes the preflight row DURABLY (synchronous write_dataset) BEFORE place_order is even called (continuous_demo.py:747-754). So if the thread is killed between place_order and the final trade-close write, the orders ledger ALREADY contains {order_link_id, status:"submitted", submit_mode:"preflight"} for that exit. The drift is narrowed to: trades row not flipped to "closed" while the venue is actually flat (position still shows open in the ledger).
- That residual is exactly what ws_risk reconcile is built to repair: reconcile_pending_order_fills / reconcile_flat_pending_exit_orders / _reconcile_pending_order_fills (ws_risk.py:525-530) handle submitted-but-unconfirmed exits, and the order is reduce_only (cannot flip the position). The in-flight guards (live_exit_syms + the ledger exit_order_link_id guard, continuous_demo.py:1236-1256) also prevent a duplicate cover on restart.
- So worst case is transient, self-healing ledger lag on the next reconcile pass on a demo/paper-only sleeve — no real-money exposure, no double-submit, no unbounded order. That is low, not medium; the venue-vs-ledger drift the finding describes is mostly pre-recorded by the preflight write and routinely reconciled. It is still a genuine correctness/robustness wart (an order-submitting thread should not be given a smaller, non-budget-aware drain window than the cache-warmer), so is_real=true.
verdict.fix_notes:
The proposed fix is directionally correct and side-effect-safe. request_shutdown() already sets _tick_event (continuous_demo_daemon.py:222-225) and the loop checks _shutdown after every wait, so a longer join only changes the WAIT CEILING when a submit is genuinely in flight — it does not delay the common (idle) case, which still drains in well under a second. No test asserts the 5.0 value (grep of tests/ found none) and no caller depends on it, so widening it is low-risk.

Concrete recommendation:
1. Enlarge the join budget to cover one exit batch's submit+fill-confirm window instead of a flat 5.0. There is no single budget constant analogous to _kline_warm_budget_seconds here; a bounded value like max(5.0, order_fill_confirm_seconds * N + margin) or a simple fixed ~20-30s ceiling is adequate (the batch is bounded by the held-position count). Mirror the _stop_kline_warmer comment so the intent is clear.
2. (Preferred, cheaper, and fully sufficient) Add an early-out: check self._shutdown.is_set() at the top of _run_protective_exit_check (before acquiring _cycle_mutex / building the trade router) so once shutdown is requested no NEW submit cycle starts. This bounds the residual window to AT MOST one in-flight batch rather than risking a fresh batch racing the join. This is a 2-line, behavior-narrowing guard with no downside.
Doing (2) alone closes the practical window; (1)+(2) together is belt-and-suspenders. Both are safe.

Caveat: do not attempt to interrupt a place_order already in flight — that is the irreducible window; the right move is simply to (a) not start new submits post-shutdown and (b) give the current one room to finish + record durably so reconcile has the full trail.

title: Binance taker-flow and OI normalizers coerce missing numeric fields to 0.0, fabricating real zeros instead of nulls
evidence: _normalize_binance_open_interest uses float(row.get('sumOpenInterest', 0.0)) / float(row.get('sumOpenInterestValue', 0.0)); _normalize_binance_taker_flow uses float(row.get('buyVol', 0.0)) etc. If the API returns a row missing these keys (schema drift, partial row), the value is silently coerced to 0.0 — a real zero open-interest / zero flow — rather than null. Downstream OI-change and imbalance features then see a spurious 0 (and a 0->next-value jump), corrupting the derived return/imbalance series. A fabricated 0.0 is undetectable as missing data, unlike a null.
impact: alpha: spurious zeros in OI/flow series produce false signal spikes (OI dropping to 0 then recovering reads as a massive OI contraction). Silent, undetectable by null-coverage checks.
proposed_fix: Use a strict accessor returning None for missing keys (like _float_or_none) and let downstream treat null as missing; only default to 0.0 for genuinely additive-absent fields. Raise on unexpected missing keys during a serious build.

verdict.reasoning:
Mechanism confirmed in code. `_normalize_binance_open_interest` (downloaders.py:756-767) does `float(row.get('sumOpenInterest', 0.0))` / `float(row.get('sumOpenInterestValue', 0.0))`, and `_normalize_binance_taker_flow` (770-789) does `float(row.get('buyVol', 0.0))` / `float(row.get('sellVol', 0.0))` / `float(row.get('buySellRatio', 0.0))`. A missing key is silently coerced to a real 0.0 rather than null.

The downstream corruption path is real and traceable: `volume_events_features._open_interest_feature_frame` (volume_events_features.py:219-258) does `.drop_nulls(['symbol','ts_ms','open_interest'])` (line 224) then computes `open_interest / open_interest.shift(1) - 1.0` (lines 239-256). A genuine `None` would be DROPPED by drop_nulls (correct), but a fabricated `0.0` survives, yielding `0/prev-1 = -1.0` on the bad day and `real/0-1 = +inf` on the next — exactly the spurious-OI-contraction-then-recovery artifact the finding describes. A fabricated 0.0 is invisible to null-coverage checks; that part of the impact claim is legitimate. For taker flow, buy=sell=0 → total=0 → taker_imbalance falls back to 0.0 (a real-looking neutral), silently masking a missing row.

Two facts pull severity DOWN to low, not medium:
1. No concrete current trigger. The endpoints hit are Binance `/futures/data/openInterestHist` and `/futures/data/takerlongshortRatio`, whose documented schemas always include these keys. The `.get(..., 0.0)` default only fires under schema drift / partial-row corruption — hypothetical, not observed. There is no code path that currently produces missing keys.
2. Dormant in the deployed strategy. The promoted SHORT profile (`event_demo._demo_event_config(profile='promoted')`, event_demo.py:1568-1583) leaves every OI/taker filter at its wide-open default (open_interest_return_*_min=-10.0/max=10.0, taker_imbalance_*_min=-1.0/max=1.0 — volume_events.py:172-185). Those defaults make the filters non-binding and SKIPPED (volume_events_filters.py:430,435,452,457 gate on `min>-10.0 or max<10.0`). So a spurious zero cannot change a live trade selection today. The real exposure is confined to research sweeps that tighten these thresholds and the `taker_imbalance_weighted` weighting mode — i.e. it could silently corrupt research/backtest results, not live execution.

Net: a genuine, silent, undetectable-by-null-checks data-integrity gap (correctly identified), but latent (no firing trigger) and not engaged by the deployed profile — low.
verdict.fix_notes:
The proposed direction is sound and the safe helper already exists: `_float_or_none` (downloaders.py:902-903) is the established same-file pattern, already used by the tickers/instruments normalizers (lines 824-869). Downstream is null-compatible: `_open_interest_feature_frame` already `drop_nulls(['open_interest'])`, parquet storage stores nulls fine in Float64 columns, and the taker `total > 0` guard already yields a clean fallback. So swapping the OI fields (`open_interest`, `open_interest_value`) to `_float_or_none(row.get(...))` is a drop-in safe change.

One IMPORTANT caveat for whoever applies it: do NOT blindly swap the taker-flow buyVol/sellVol. They feed arithmetic — `buy_volume + sell_volume`, `buy_volume - sell_volume` (downloaders.py:775,782). If those become `None`, `None + None` raises TypeError, changing a silent-zero bug into a crash. The fix must either (a) skip/emit-null the whole row when buyVol/sellVol are absent, or (b) keep additive 0.0 ONLY for genuinely-additive flow fields while guarding the imbalance/ratio. The `buy_sell_ratio` field is the clean case to switch to `_float_or_none` directly. Also note the analogous Bybit `_normalize_open_interest` (downloaders.py:804-814) has the same `.get(..., 0.0)` pattern — fix both for consistency, since the Bybit OI is the one actually wired into the live universe path.

The finding's secondary suggestion to 'raise on unexpected missing keys during a serious build' is a reasonable hardening but a design choice, not required for correctness; null-coercion + the existing drop_nulls already removes the corruption. Recommend pairing the change with a unit test that feeds a partial row and asserts the field is null (and dropped), since there is no existing test covering missing-key behavior for these two normalizers.

title: MS_PER_DAY / MS_PER_HOUR redefined as literals in 3+ modules instead of importing from _common
evidence: _common.py:20-21 defines MS_PER_HOUR=3_600_000 and MS_PER_DAY=86_400_000, but risk_model.py:57 (`MS_PER_DAY = 86_400_000`), signal_harness.py:41-42 (MS_PER_DAY + MS_PER_HOUR), and continuous_events.py uses a local MS_PER_DAY for day-flooring (continuous_events.py:220).
